query: Starting from a eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical microstructure of dual-phase lamellar colonies, what single intervention could overcome limited room-temperature tensile ductility and brittleness while retaining or increasing strength? The hypothesis should address the tendency for dislocation pile-ups near internal boundaries to produce local stress concentrations, microcracking, and catastrophic damage during straining. Specify the intervention, its mechanism, the predicted strength and ductility relative to the untreated starting material, the applicable testing and operating conditions, supporting prior evidence, and a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A short-duration, intermediate‐temperature annealing treatment applied post-deformation can re‐engineer the lamellar interfaces—by promoting fine-scale recovery and localized solute segregation—to reduce dislocation pile‐up and stress concentration, thereby overcoming room‑temperature brittleness while retaining or even increasing the strength.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast eutectic high-entropy alloy with a hierarchical dual-phase lamellar (e.g., FCC + B2 or L12) microstructure.
generation.intervention: A single-step annealing treatment at an intermediate temperature (approximately 600–700 °C) after a deformation (e.g., cold rolling or cryo-rolling) to partially relieve stored strain energy and trigger controlled interfacial modification.
generation.conditions: Quasi-static room-temperature tensile tests on bulk specimens; processing in ambient atmosphere with a rapid heating–cooling cycle to retain fine lamellar geometry.
generation.structural_mediator: Refined lamellar colonies with ultrathin, solute-enriched (e.g., Cr) interphase boundaries and a heterogeneous microstructure that supports a mix of ultrafine recrystallized grains in one phase and less-recrystallized regions in the other.
generation.mechanism: The annealing induces localized recovery and limited precipitation at the lamellar interfaces. This enhances chemical segregation (or ordering) at the internal boundaries, which smooths out the dislocation pile-ups by creating interfaces that both block dislocation transmission and deflect stress concentrations. The resulting interfaces thus arrest microcrack formation while the background ultrafine microstructure retains or even improves strength.
generation.predicted_outcome: An increase in room-temperature tensile ductility (e.g., higher elongation-to-failure compared to the untreated state) while maintaining or slightly increasing yield and ultimate tensile strengths relative to baseline values of the as-cast EHEA.
generation.baseline: The untreated eutectic high-entropy alloy typically shows high strength (e.g., a yield strength around 750 MPa) but limited ductility (approximately 18% elongation) due to dislocation pile-ups at semi-coherent lamellar interfaces.
generation.boundary: This improvement is expected under quasi-static, room-temperature deformation; the effect may be less pronounced at substantially higher strain rates or temperatures where interface stability and dynamic recovery mechanisms differ.
generation.uncertainty: While studies (e.g., PMC6175879 and PMC5818523) have noted that inherent chemical disorder and cryo-rolling/annealing treatments can yield hierarchically heterogeneous structures with strong interfaces, it is uncertain if a single annealing step can reliably produce the optimal solute segregation and interface modification needed to alleviate dislocation pile-ups in all eutectic HEA systems.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of eutectic HEA samples: one set processed by the proposed deformation step (e.g., cold or cryo-rolling) followed by the intermediate-temperature annealing treatment, and a control group that is deformed but not annealed. Characterize their microstructures (using TEM and APT/EDS for chemical segregation) and perform room-temperature quasi-static tensile tests.
measurements: Interphase boundary chemistry/segregation (via APT or high-resolution EDS)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the annealed samples do not exhibit a statistically significant improvement in tensile ductility compared to the control group—without a corresponding drop in strength—or if microstructural analysis fails to show evidence of modified (i.e. solute-enriched or roughened) interfaces that reduce dislocation pile-ups, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Nano-lamellar (L12 + B2) AlCoCrFeNi2.1 eutectic high entropy alloy (EHEA) was processed by cryo-rolling and annealing. The EHEA developed a novel hierarchical microstructure featured by fine lamellar regions consisting of FCC lamellae filled with ultrafine FCC grains (average size ~200–250 nm) and B2 lamellae, and coarse non-lamellar regions consisting of ultrafine FCC (average size ~200–250 nm), few coarse recrystallized FCC grains and rather coarse unrecrystallized B2 phase (~2.5 µm). This complex and hierarchical microstructure originated from differences in strain-partitioning amongst the constituent phases, affecting the driving force for recrystallization. The hierarchical microstructure of the cryo-rolled and annealed material resulted in simultaneous enhancement in strength (Yield Strength/YS: 1437 ± 26 MPa, Ultimate Tensile Strength/UTS: 1562 ± 33 MPa) and ductility (elongation to failure/ef ~ 14 ± 1%) as compared to the as-cast as well as cold-rolled and annealed materials. The properties of many metallic alloys are essentially related to the structure, morphology and chemical distribution of boundaries. In terms of atomic structure, the phase boundaries contained in eutectic dual-phase HEAs were supposed to be insufficient in prohibiting dislocations due to their semi-coherent nature, which is similar to those widely reported in NiAl dual-phase intermetallic alloys,. However, in-situ deformation tests revealed that dense dislocation storage can be achieved within FCC phases and dislocation walls were formed along phase boundaries. The unexpected strong interfaces are thought to be highly related to the chemically disordered distribution of multiple solution atoms at phase boundaries as well as in the matrix of HEAs. Particularly, an ultra-thin segregation zone of randomly distributed Cr atoms, typically less than 2 nm in width (Fig. 3b and S4), was detected near the phase boundary without forming complex intermetallic compounds, which were intrinsically brittle and would lead to stress concentration.
